claims.text: The local catalog, Bulbapedia volume page, PokeBoon, and Japanese bookstore metadata align on July 23, 2001 for How I Became a Pokemon Card Vol. 5 / ポケモンカードになったワケ 5.
Bulbapedia lists the first Japanese edition as Kadokawa-Media Factory, and Japanese bookstore metadata lists Media Factory as publisher with ISBN 9784889917918.
The local release family models one row: Hoppip source index 241, with the promotion note How I Became a Pokemon Card Vol. 5 insert.
Bulbapedia volume 5 lists chapters PW28-PW32 and includes The Smile that Makes Hoppip Happy, while PokeBoon identifies Hoppip and Gengar as Pokemon depicted in the card illustration.
Kagemaru Himeno is both the creator of the How I Became a Pokemon Card manga and the illustrator of the Hoppip promo, making this a creator-illustrator loop rather than a detached pack insert.
How I Became a Pokemon Card Vol. 5 matters because the manga supplies narrative context for the Hoppip card image; the card is an object whose source tells you why the picture exists.

narrative.human_title: How I Became a Pokemon Card Vol. 5 — Hoppip held to the ground by story
narrative.why_it_matters: Vol. 5 is one of the clearest expressions of what this catalog is trying to preserve. Hoppip is a tiny Pokemon famous for being so light it might blow away, and Himeno gives that lightness a story frame. The manga, the card, the open-book symbol, and the bonus-card border text all point at the same thing: this card is not merely included with a book; it is explained by the book.

narrative.human_title: Hoppip — source index 241, the light little Natta Wake card
narrative.why_it_matters: Hoppip is such a small card to carry such a perfect idea. Its Silver Pokedex text says it has to plant its feet so it will not be blown away; Himeno's manga gives that lightness a scene, a smile, and even a Gengar-shaped bit of mischief. This is exactly what Natta Wake does best: it makes the card image feel like evidence of a tiny story instead of a decorative crop.
